URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202610162840
Iran International, fetched 08:12 BST

Cooper said US operations had prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil and helped freeze nearly $350 million in cryptocurrency assets, restricting Tehran's ability to finance allied militias and rebuilding destroyed weapons facilities.

“Iran's government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits to workers in industries such as oil and energy, manufacturing, construction, security and the IRGC itself,” he said.

Cooper said there were reports that Iran-aligned militias across the region were withholding payments to their fighters to divert funds to the Revolutionary Guards. He described the IRGC as increasingly desperate and linked its financial difficulties to repeated attacks on merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz that have killed civilian sailors.

"])•••$RC("B:4","S:4")More StoriesIran raided, summoned and jailed Baha’is in Yazd 34 times in seven monthsOct 16, 2026, 18:23 GMT+1Listen to this article100%Iranian security and judicial authorities have taken action against Baha’is in the central city of Yazd at least 34 times in less than seven months, raiding homes, summoning dozens for interrogation and jailing members of the faith, the rights group HRANA reported on Friday.

Between March 28 and October 15, HRANA recorded 11 searches of homes and other property, 18 summonses for interrogation, three prison sentences and one person taken to prison to serve his term.

The targets went beyond people facing charges to guests at private gatherings and their relatives. Agents seized phones, computers, books, photographs and religious materials, and in one case a car.

On March 28, Intelligence Ministry agents broke up a gathering of about 50 Baha’is sharing a traditional soup, a local Yazd custom, and took their phones without a warrant. The phones have not been returned despite legal complaints. About 12 of those present were later summoned for questioning.

The pressure peaked in September, when six homes were searched and six people summoned. On September 27, about 40 agents searched the home of the family of Farhang Amiri, a Baha’i who was stabbed to death outside his house in Yazd on that date in 2016. The two men charged in his killing said they had attacked him because of his faith. That night agents also searched the homes of his son, daughter and son-in-law, and on October 1 they searched the family’s farm.

Flora Samadani, a Yazd resident, was sentenced by the city’s Revolutionary Court to three years and one day in prison for “deviant propaganda contrary to Islam by promoting Baha’ism.” Her husband, Ahmad Jafari Naeimi, received six months and one day for assisting her. Moein Mohammadi-Dehaj, 39, was sentenced in the summer to 16 years and seven months in prison, a 10-year loss of civil rights and a lifelong ban from public employment.

The crackdown extends well beyond Yazd. Raids on Baha’i homes since the January protests amount to “state-sponsored theft,” the Baha’i International Community’s representative to the UN in Geneva told Iran International in August, citing hundreds of incidents.

“With the misuse of their state authority, they essentially steal Baha’is’ properties with complete impunity,” Simin Fahandej said.

The community said this week that the case of 26 Baha’is in Shiraz, acquitted nearly four years ago, had been reopened, and that as of October 2 at least 64 Baha’is were in detention or prison, with 19 more serving sentences under electronic tags or on furlough. In August, 13 UN experts warned of torture, enforced disappearances and a sharp rise in persecution.

Iran’s Baha’is, estimated at more than 300,000, form the country’s largest non-Muslim minority. The constitution recognizes only Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism, and Baha’is have faced systematic persecution since the 1979 revolution, including bans from universities, business closures and property confiscations.

Listen to this article100%Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.

Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.

Ayoub Mohammad Nabil, from Haditha in western Iraq, was hanged on Sunday morning at Lakan Prison in Rasht, the capital of Gilan province on the Caspian coast, the group said. Iranian officials and domestic media had not reported his sentence or his execution by the time it was announced.

Nabil had entered Iran legally on his passport and was working as a caretaker at a private villa when Intelligence Ministry agents arrested him in the nearby town of Fouman on August 26, 2025. He had no prior security record, Iran Human Rights said.

A source told the group he was held for about five months at the Intelligence Ministry’s detention center in Rasht, where he was subjected to severe psychological torture. He denied any link to Saudi Arabia or groups tied to it, and said he had been accused because he was a practicing Sunni Muslim, wore a beard and taught the Quran to local children in his guardhouse.

Despite no evidence of any political activity, the source said, Branch One of Rasht’s Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death for “moharebeh,” or waging war against God, through spying for Saudi-backed proxy groups.

The Kurdish rights group Hengaw, citing its own sources, said Nabil was moved to solitary confinement for execution on October 8, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis intensified.

He is at least the 17th person executed in Iran on espionage charges this year, and the third Iraqi, according to Iran Human Rights. Thirteen were accused of spying for Israel or the United States; the other two Iraqis were accused of spying for an unnamed Arab country, and an Afghan man for an unnamed state. Fifteen of the 17 were executed after the war began in February.

More than 70 political prisoners have been executed in Iran since the January protests, and at least 20 more face execution on political charges, Iran International has found.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a report on Thursday that capital cases in Iran, especially security cases, involve systematic violations of fair-trial rights, including forced confessions, closed trials lasting minutes and restricted access to independent lawyers. He called for an immediate halt to executions.

The rights group HRANA said last week that at least 2,003 people were executed in Iran in the year to October 8, up 29 percent on the previous year.

Listen to this article100%Former US diplomat Joey Hood during an interview at Iran International’s studio in Washington.Decades of American sanctions strengthened Iran’s Revolutionary Guards by hollowing out the middle class, former US diplomat Joey Hood told Iran International, and once the fighting ends, Tehran will face a reckoning with its own people.

Hood, who retired earlier this year after 27 years in the Foreign Service, served as acting assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs, deputy chief of mission in Iraq and Kuwait, and US ambassador to Tunisia. He spoke in a studio interview.

He called the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979 and the 444-day hostage crisis that followed “the very definition of evil,” adding that the protection of envoys is an ancient principle recognized in Islamic tradition as well.

What followed, he said, was a pattern. In 1983, a suicide bombing at the US Marine barracks in Beirut killed 241 American service members who had been deployed as peacekeepers; US courts have found Iran responsible for the attack, carried out by militants who went on to form Hezbollah. In 1996, the Khobar Towers housing complex in Saudi Arabia was bombed; US investigators blamed Saudi Hezbollah (Hezbollah Al-Hejaz), acting with Iranian support. In 2011, US prosecutors charged an Iranian-American man with plotting, on behalf of the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, to assassinate the Saudi ambassador in Washington. Argentina’s courts have held Iran responsible for the 1994 bombing of a Jewish center in Buenos Aires, and plots have been traced to Iran in Europe and Asia.

None of it, Hood said, has won the Islamic Republic a single endorsement.

“You haven’t seen any other country come out and say, ‘What the Iranian regime is doing is great,’” he said. “There’s no sovereign government anywhere in the world that has made such a declaration.”

Successive US administrations from Carter to Obama tried various forms of engagement, Hood said, but repeatedly underestimated Tehran’s refusal to accept normal relations. Even when presidents saw the risks, they often stopped short of decisive action. Jimmy Carter understood the danger before admitting the exiled Shah to the United States for cancer treatment in October 1979, weeks before the embassy was seized. After the Beirut bombing, Ronald Reagan withdrew the Marines and limited the American response largely to sanctions, a choice Hood said emboldened Tehran.

Analysts warned as early as the Obama years, Hood said, that sanctions were “squeezing out the normal middle-class businessmen and women and handing the economy over to a shadowy black-market economy” run by the Revolutionary Guards. That has come true, he said: the Guards grew stronger and the middle class weaker, and that middle class has periodically taken to the streets.

The Islamic Republic drew its own lesson from the fall of the Shah, whose government collapsed after months of protest, Hood said. It keeps using lethal force until protests stop, as it did in 2009, 2019 and January 2026.

Congress favors sanctions because they appear to cost no American lives, Hood said, “but Iranian lives certainly are at stake, especially for the middle class and the poor.”

Money is also fungible. Relief that came with the 2015 nuclear deal, he said, went to regional militias rather than public welfare, with particularly deadly results in Syria. Hood declined to use the name Hezbollah, which means “Party of God” in Arabic, calling the group “Iran’s militia in Lebanon.” “God does not have a political party here on Earth, and certainly not a militia,” he said.

Coalitions, not bilateral deals

A more effective approach, Hood said, would press on the nuclear program and the militia network at the same time, with allies rather than through bilateral arrangements.

Under Obama, near-unanimous support in Congress for sanctions helped bring even Russia and China along on the nuclear file. Without that kind of coalition, he said, constraints stay limited. The bilateral agreements the current administration has made with Saudi Arabia, Syria and others help partners defend themselves, but isolating Tehran needs broader coordination.

He tied the Houthis’ recent escalation against Saudi Arabia to Tehran’s difficulty moving fuel and running its shadow fleet under US pressure, and said the Yemeni group would pose no comparable threat without Iranian support. With less leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, he said, Tehran and its allies have turned to other targets, among them Saudi Arabia and potentially the Bab el-Mandeb strait or the Suez Canal.

October, ahead of the US midterm elections, is a period of heightened risk, he said, given the Islamic Republic’s record of trying to influence American votes.

The decisive change since the 12-day war in June 2025, Hood said, is that “anything that Iran or its militias do around the world will be answered for in Iran.” Earlier presidents avoided direct confrontation and preferred to fight Tehran’s proxies.

“That’s the big difference now,” he said. “Iranians themselves are having to pay for Iran’s foreign policy for the first time.”

When active military operations end, Hood said, he expects a reckoning between the Islamic Republic and its own people. Without a lasting coalition to constrain it, he said, the confrontation that began in 1979 will go on in new phases, with more attacks on American interests and partners.

Iran managed to export jet fuel to Myanmar and send several shipments of liquefied petroleum gas out of the region despite a US naval blockade that has largely halted its crude exports, Reuters reported on Friday.

Satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax showed a tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, Reuters said.
